Telecommunication conversational application

Role: conversational AI designer · Mix, Visio · Voice application

My role

I owned the broadcast message and schedule a callback features of a new voice application, taking each from high-level flowchart to a build in Mix. I worked with conversational AI designers, speech scientists, developers, QA specialists and project managers.

The mandate

Build a new application on the Mix platform that fits the existing backend and integrates into the company’s environment. It shipped in four releases over one year, with a third-party development partner.

Design process

  • Kickoff and business goals
  • Voice persona, limitations and features
  • Research: business documents, developers, current website and services
  • High-level design: user journeys and flowcharts
  • Feedback and iteration with collaborators
  • Build in Mix: flows, backend integration, error handling
  • QA: test calls and recovery paths
  • Customer demo and approval of design and prompts

Design decisions

  • Recovery built in. Prompts use yes/no questions and answer options, with keypad (DTMF) as a backup.
  • Broadcast message. Configurable prompts the business can customize, then routing to goodbye, transfer, self-service or the main menu based on customer profile and behavior.
  • Schedule a callback. Callers choose a day, then a time span, then a slot, which reduces agent transfers and escalations. The existing API and fixed calendar shaped the design.
  • Reuse. The application builds on the company’s existing working APIs.

Deliverables: Visio flowcharts, the low-level design as an HTML file of the application, a prompt list and a stakeholder presentation.

Schedule a callback

Reduce transfers by helping callers choose an available day and time, then confirming the callback.

  1. Identify the callerConfirm or collect a reusable callback number.
  2. Check existing appointmentsAvoid duplicate bookings and explain available options.
  3. Select a dayOffer only days returned by the calendar service.
  4. Select a timePresent one, two, or three available slots in natural language.
  5. Confirm the callbackRepeat the selected date, time, and callback number.
  6. Recover gracefullyRetry when useful, then return or transfer if scheduling fails.
Example prompt

“Looking at the calendar, I have three times available: 3:00, 4:30, and 5:00. Which time works best for you?”

Healthcare IVR

Role: design lead · Full IVR application experience

My role

I led the design team in designing the full application experience and presented the work to stakeholders.

The task

Design the phone flow that verifies a customer’s eight-digit activation code so they can unlock their pharmacy account online.

What the flow handles

  • Caller ID check, with a transfer when it isn’t available.
  • Code entry with read-back confirmation (press 1 or 2).
  • A maximum of three retries, then a transfer.
  • Different spoken messages for each API result code.

How I worked

I split the flow into reusable components (Main, PIN, Transfer, Goodbye) and documented the API return values, including the status codes for unregistered phone, invalid key and locked key, so each outcome had its own prompt. I also flagged open questions for the team, such as which routing data is needed before a transfer and whether a success code could be confirmed from the API.

Airway voice assistant

Role: conversation designer · Voiceflow

My role

I designed the call flow in Voiceflow: the experience principles, the conversation paths, the error handling and the wording, and I presented my reasoning.

The brief

A start-up airline with a cool, fresh vibe wanted to automate phone support. The task: tell callers how to prepare for bringing a pet in the cabin, using voice recognition only.

Experience principles

  • A reply within 6 seconds, with no dead air.
  • Fresh background music while callers wait.
  • A clear voice that flows naturally.

Decisions I made and why

  • Language setting up front because customers may speak more than one language, rather than assuming English.
  • Repeat option and extra categories for callers who lose focus or have a question outside the menu, plus a route to customer service.
  • Utterances like “pet fees”, “cabin cost”, “pet travelling price” so people can say it their own way, with a confirm step to catch recognition errors.
  • Plain wording for pet owners instead of airline terms like “stowed”, and fees separated from exceptions so answers stay short.
  • An offer to hear it again, based on the assumption that callers hang up once they have what they need.

Human-AI collaboration in group creativity

Role: lead researcher and UX designer · MSc thesis, HEC Montréal

My role

Visio and Nuance Mix applications.

The question

Most chatbot research looks at one-on-one customer service. I studied what happens when a chatbot joins a remote team brainstorm: does the chatbot’s conversational style and its role change how creative the group is?

The method

An online 2×2 between-subject experiment run with the Wizard of Oz technique, where a human plays the chatbot from a script. Groups wrote slogans for public transport. The four bots were human or machine in style, facilitator or ideator in role.

Who took part

190 participants in 61 groups of 2–4, recruited through Prolific. Creativity was measured by self-report, idea quantity and expert-rated idea quality, with serendipity measured on a validated scale.

“Serendipity: an unexpected ‘aha’ moment during problem-solving or idea generation.”

McCay-Peet et al., 2015

What I found

  • Human-style bots led to higher idea quality.
  • Machine-style bots and facilitator roles led to more ideas.
  • Facilitator plus human style gave the best-quality ideas.
  • Ideator bots felt more serendipitous, but that did not show up in the output within a short session.

Why it matters for design

Chatbot tone and role involve a trade-off between quantity and quality of ideas. Teams should pick the bot personality for the creative goal. Limits: scripted replies, small sample, short time frame. The work was published as a TREO conference paper.

Government website UX research report

Role: UX consultant · Usability study of a bilingual government website

My role

As part of a research team, I ran usability testing and contributed UX recommendations for a government website.

The question

How well can English-speaking users with different levels of French find information on a bilingual government website, and where do they hit friction? We looked at usefulness, effectiveness and efficiency.

The method

16 participants in two groups of 8, split by French level. Each did three counterbalanced tasks: a popular page (find a health center phone number), a broken journey (find financial support for farming) and a deep page (find a fishing permit cost). Measures included success, steps, time, NASA-TLX, effort scores, WebQual and interviews.

What we found

  • No significant difference between the two French-level groups.
  • All 16 participants needed help on the broken journey. None thought to switch to the French site, where the information lived.
  • Once on the French site, people found it in about three clicks, whatever their French level.
  • Some labels confused users, such as health services versus health resources, and some buttons looked like titles.

What we recommended

  • Urgent: tell users, on the homepage and inner pages, when information exists only in French.
  • Short term: offer multiple routes to the same information for different mental models, and rename confusing labels.
  • Longer term: add a mega menu or a chatbot, and sub-links on the health page.

Cook It startup UX research report

Role: UX consultant · Usability study with 16 participants

My role

As part of a four-person research team, I developed the research plan, ran usability sessions and presented insights to the client.

The mandate

Evaluate how first-time users experience a meal kit startup on mobile and web: do they understand the service, subscribe, order a first box and react to the promo code? For ethical reasons, subscribing and ordering ran on a mirror of the live site.

The hypothesis

First-time users with prior experience of competing meal kit services would subscribe and order faster than users with none.

The method

A between-subject experiment with 16 participants (8 men, 8 women, average age 26.5), about an hour each: three tasks with post-task interviews and questionnaires. Data came from video, semi-structured interviews and Google Forms, using SEQ, CSAT, CES, NASA-TLX, SUS and WebQual.

What we found

  • 14 of 16 fully or partly understood the service from the homepage.
  • 16 of 16 subscribed and found it easy. Ordering a first box was easy but satisfaction was low.
  • No significant difference between users with and without prior experience.
  • Users liked the colors and would keep using it on mobile, but wanted an app.

What we recommended

  • High priority: keep the color scheme, and cut homepage scrolling by removing content and adding filters.
  • Flow: let users see the menu before paying, add a pantry explanation and breadcrumbs, and make the confirmation step clearer.
  • Forms: stop auto-capitalizing email fields, add a show-password option, make the promo code editable and auto-applied, and replace the sideways-scrolling calendar.
  • Homepage: add pricing to build interest.

Fresh Tooth, a dental hygiene game app

Role: UX researcher and designer · UX report for Doctor & Gambit’s

My role

I ran the research and concept work and presented the report: the interview and persona, the design thinking workshop, the final concept and the customer journey.

The question

How might we support and delight customers through a better dental hygiene routine, without putting all the investment into a physical product?

Research

An interview-based persona (Kathy, 22, a student worried about waste and cost), then a design thinking workshop with 4 participants and 2 designers using warm-up, value proposition, Crazy 8 and alter ego activities.

The concept

An educational game app, reachable from the brand’s website, that teaches eco-friendly dental care through quiz-style play. I mapped Kathy’s journey, including the stress at each decision, and listed design opportunities such as an intuitive swipe interaction, no more than two or four options per question, and bookmarks for key facts. Next steps: usability testing, then content and level development.
